title: MA8-16074
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, Mr. XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, a citizen of El Salvador, is claiming refugee protection in Canada under section 96 and paragraph 97(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
Here is a summary of the claimant's allegations, as they appear in his Personal Information Form (PIF).

The claimant was working for a XXXXX XXXXX in El Salvador. In XXXXX 2008, he was required, under threat of death, to pay a monthly amount of one hundred dollars to members of the Mara Salvatrucha gang. The claimant and his family were subjected to threats and intimidation. His wife and children left to live in Honduras. The claimant left his country on XXXXX, 2008.
The claimant's identity was established to the panel's satisfaction by the exhibits filed on the record.1

Having examined the documentary and testimonial evidence, the panel determines that the claimant is not a person in need of protection or a Convention refugee, for the following reasons. Claim under section 96 of the IRPA

In order to benefit from protection under section 96, the claimant must demonstrate that there is a serious possibility that he would be persecuted if he were to return to his country, by reason of one of the five grounds under the Geneva Convention: race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership in a particular social group. The panel is of the opinion that the claimant did not support his fear of persecution with evidence related to one of the five grounds of the Convention. Claim under paragraph 97(1)(a) of the IRPA

The claimant's evidence did not implicate El Salvador or one of its agents as the agent of persecution. Accordingly, the panel finds that the claim cannot be considered under paragraph 97(1)(a) of the IRPA. Claim under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA
Is the claimant at a higher personalized risk than that of the general population in El Salvador, within the meaning of Prophète?2

The claimant stated that he fears 15 members of the Mara Salvatrucha, and that they operate in the neighbourhood where he was living. He knew them before they approached him in XXXXX 2008, when they allegedly began extorting from him. The claimant stated that he was approached because he held a position at a XXXXX XXXXX; it was therefore easier to obtain money from him. He was in charge of XXXXX and XXXXX. When questioned as to whether he faced the same risk as other citizens, the claimant responded that the risk was the same and that everyone in the general population is at risk of being extorted by gangs. He added that citizens must pay, failing which they might be killed-this is what he fears. When asked whether he could live somewhere else, like San Salvador, the claimant stated that he would be at risk of being extorted there as well, either by the Mara Salvatrucha or by the M-18, because the gangs are everywhere.

Therefore, the claimant's risk of being targeted and extorted is the same as that faced by other citizens of El Salvador. The claimant indicated that it was easier to target him because he worked for a XXXXX XXXXX.

The documentation, in this case, tab 7.6 of the National Documentation Package on El Salvador,3 indicates that El Salvador is one of the most dangerous countries in the world. According to the World Health Organization's criteria, there is an epidemic of murders, and young men are the principal target of assailants.

There are about 100 gangs in El Salvador, comprising 30,000 members. They kill, steal and extort from anyone in order to be able to support their incarcerated associates and their family. Businesses and farming operations are extortion targets. Home burglary is becoming more prevalent, as is credit card cloning and kidnapping for ransom. Cyber crime also exists. The documentary evidence demonstrates that every stratum of society is affected and that all citizens are at risk of being victims of criminality.

In this context, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant's fear is a generalized fear that is also faced by the general population in El Salvador, who must live and cope with the torments of criminality and the consequences of the proliferation of gangs.4

The issue of generalized risk is a principle that case law confirmed in Prophète.5 In that case, Honourable Madam Justice Tremblay-Lamer stated that, when in a country, the risk of being targeted by any form of criminality is general; this does not constitute a risk of being subjected to a risk to life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA.
The panel is of the opinion that the claimant did not demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, that he faced a personalized risk and a greater risk than the population in general.
As a result, the panel determines that it cannot allow the claim filed by the claimant under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA.

For the reasons previously provided, the panel rejects the claim filed by XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, and does not recognize him as a Convention refugee under section 96 or a person in need of protection under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

Accordingly, his claim for refugee protection is rejected.
